sessions.name: Norwegian 4×4
sessions.desc: Four 4-minute efforts at 85–95% of max heart rate with 3 easy minutes between. One of the best-studied workouts for VO₂max and heart health. On the bike, stay seated and push cadence rather than grinding heavy resistance.

sessions.name: Travel-day reset

sessions.name: Murph builder
sessions.desc: Murph is 1 mile, 100 pull-ups, 200 push-ups, 300 squats, 1 mile. Build it in rounds of 5 pull · 10 push · 15 squat — 20 rounds is the full volume. Add a round each time; Phase 1 caps at 10 rounds to spare the knees.

sessions.name: Cindy
sessions.desc: As many rounds as possible in 20 minutes of 5 pull · 10 push · 15 squat. Test it once a month — the rounds number is your Murph fitness in one figure. In Phase 1, stop at 10 rounds even if time remains.

timer.label: 5 pull · 10 push · 15 squat — as many rounds as possible

sessions.name: Murph

fastingStages.name: Fed
fastingStages.desc: Digesting your last meal. Blood sugar and insulin are up and your body is storing energy.

fastingStages.name: Early fast
fastingStages.desc: Insulin is falling. Your liver releases stored glycogen to keep blood sugar steady, and fat-burning starts to ramp up.

fastingStages.name: Metabolic switch
fastingStages.desc: Somewhere between about 12 and 36 hours (sooner if you trained or ate low-carb), liver glycogen runs low, fat becomes the main fuel and the liver starts making ketones.

fastingStages.name: Ketones rising
fastingStages.desc: Ketone levels are climbing (full ketosis often arrives nearer 24 hours or later). Hunger tends to come in waves around your usual mealtimes, then pass. Growth hormone tends to rise during a fast, which may help spare muscle.

fastingStages.name: Deep fast
fastingStages.desc: Liver glycogen is largely spent (muscle keeps its own stores), so you're running mostly on fat with ketones climbing; the brain still runs mainly on glucose your liver makes. Cellular clean-up (autophagy) is thought to ramp up — the strongest evidence is from animal studies, and the human timing isn't pinned down.

fastingStages.name: Top of your range
fastingStages.desc: You're at the top of the 24–36 h range. Break the fast with a protein-forward, normal-sized meal.

fastingTips: Water, black coffee, plain tea and electrolytes (a pinch of salt, magnesium) are fine. Check with your doctor before adding potassium if you take blood-pressure medication or have kidney disease.
Skip ibuprofen and naproxen on an empty stomach — they're hard on the gut lining.
Keep training easy — walk, PT, mobility. Save heavy lifting and 4×4s for fed days.
Stand up slowly. Brief light-headedness is common; real dizziness, palpitations or confusion mean end the fast and eat.
Break it with protein and a normal-sized meal, not a feast.
fastingCaution: Skip fasting if you take diabetes medication (especially insulin or sulfonylureas), blood-pressure medication or diuretics, have kidney disease or gout, are underweight or unwell, or have a history of disordered eating — check with your doctor first.

pain.text: OK if it settles within 24 hours and there's no extra knee swelling the next morning — but don't add load or range until it does.
Stop that exercise. Swap it, or finish with a recovery session.

flags.title: Knee
items: A knee that locks and stays locked (won't fully straighten) — don't force it and don't train on it. See a doctor or orthopedist the same or next day: with a bucket-handle tear it can mean the torn piece has flipped, and that's time-sensitive.
Catching, giving way, or new swelling — stop the session and call your PT.

flags.title: Lower back
items: Numbness in the saddle area (genitals, anus, buttocks, inner thighs), new trouble starting or controlling urine, bowel leakage, new sexual dysfunction, or sciatica down both legs — go to emergency care now.
Leg weakness that's getting worse, or foot drop (the front of the foot slapping or catching as you walk) — see a doctor promptly.
Pain, numbness or tingling travelling further down a leg — stop and check in with your PT or doctor.

flags.title: Heart
items: Chest pain or pressure, unusual breathlessness, palpitations or feeling faint during cardio (especially 4×4s) — stop. If chest pain doesn't settle within a few minutes of stopping, call emergency services.

safety.general: Forge is a training log and planner, not medical advice. Show your PT the plan — every exercise can be swapped, and the injury filters are a starting point, not a clearance.
